content:
iOS 27 Beta 5 contains a reference to an upcoming feature that will let Apple verify the authenticity of photos taken on iPhone.

While this isn't a feature that many iPhone users will need to use, as we'll get to shortly, it's just the start...

What is Apple Reference Images?

AI-generated images and videos are advancing rapidly, becoming more sophisticated and realistic, sometimes making it genuinely difficult to tell whether a photo was genuinely taken. This is being exploited by scammers and those seeking to spread disinformation.

An industry body has been set up to tackle this issue, called the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA). This offers ways to identify genuine photos and let viewers see the edit history, whether or not AI tools were used.

Over 500 companies have signed up to the C2PA programme, but Apple now appears to be going it alone with its Apple Reference Images (ARI) feature. Anyone taking a photo on iPhone with ARI enabled can upload the photo to Apple's servers to be verified as genuine.

Why is this only the start?

Resources found in the latest beta show that ARI is off by default, because the vast majority of iPhone users will never need it. The feature is primarily aimed at journalists and those involved in legal proceedings, who might need independent evidence that the photos they take are genuine.

While the initial use of ARI may be limited, this type of feature is likely to become more common as AI image generation becomes more prevalent. For example, the EU recently published a code of practice regarding transparency around AI-generated content, to make it easier for the public to tell whether content is real. This covers both images and text (see below).

This is currently voluntary, but AI heavyweights have already read the writing on the wall and announced their support. Anthropic has said that all future versions of Claude will add digital watermarks to both text and images. Notably, the company will be rolling this out globally, not just in EU nations—which somewhat suggests that this type of requirement is likely to become mandatory worldwide in the not-too-distant future.

How can text be verified?

Perhaps the most striking aspect of the EU's measure is that it requires AI companies to add digital watermarks to text output, just as they do with images.

This can be done using characters that aren't visible to the naked eye—for example, between the words 'invisible' and 'characters' in this sentence, I've used a replacement for the space. These characters are preserved if you copy and paste, but are trivially defeated by optical character recognition (OCR) methods. For example, I have a tool on my Mac that lets me do this as easily as taking a screenshot (which I have installed because some companies, astonishingly, like to post statements to social media as images).

It has been suggested that Anthropic may go further by using specific language patterns to mark Claude's output, so that even OCR'd text can be detected. I have plenty of thoughts on this, but they're beyond the scope of this article.

If these kinds of measures do end up becoming mandatory, Apple will need to apply them to features such as its Siri AI rewrites.

What do you think about this trend? Let me know in the comments.
